answer_text:
Let \(a_n\) be the given sequence. We need \(a_{2000} \pmod 9\).

Since we only care about remainders modulo \(9\), we can work with

\[
b_n \equiv a_n \pmod 9.
\]

The recurrence remains

\[
b_n \equiv 2b_{n-1}+2b_{n-2} \pmod 9.
\]

Now compute the first several terms modulo \(9\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
b_1 &= 1,\\
b_2 &= 3,\\
b_3 &\equiv 2(3+1)=8 \pmod 9,\\
b_4 &\equiv 2(8+3)=22 \equiv 4 \pmod 9,\\
b_5 &\equiv 2(4+8)=24 \equiv 6 \pmod 9,\\
b_6 &\equiv 2(6+4)=20 \equiv 2 \pmod 9,\\
b_7 &\equiv 2(2+6)=16 \equiv 7 \pmod 9,\\
b_8 &\equiv 2(7+2)=18 \equiv 0 \pmod 9,\\
b_9 &\equiv 2(0+7)=14 \equiv 5 \pmod 9,\\
b_{10} &\equiv 2(5+0)=10 \equiv 1 \pmod 9,\\
b_{11} &\equiv 2(1+5)=12 \equiv 3 \pmod 9.
\end{aligned}
\]

We see that

\[
(b_{10},b_{11}) \equiv (b_1,b_2) \pmod 9.
\]

Because the recurrence determines the next term from the previous two terms, the sequence of remainders repeats with period \(10\).

Since

\[
2000 \equiv 0 \pmod{10},
\]

we have

\[
b_{2000} \equiv b_{10} \equiv 1 \pmod 9.
\]

Therefore, the remainder is

\[
\boxed{1}
\]
